==Problem==
A pair of fair <imath>6</imath>-sided dice is rolled <imath>n</imath> times. What is the least value of <imath>n</imath> such that the probability that the sum of the numbers face up on a roll equals <imath>7</imath> at least once is greater than <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 2 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 3 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 4 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 5 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 6</imath>

==Solution 1 (Complement)==
Rolling a pair of fair <imath>6</imath>-sided dice, the probability of getting a sum of <imath>7</imath> is <imath>\frac16:</imath> Regardless what the first die shows, the second die has exactly one outcome to make the sum <imath>7.</imath> We consider the complement: The probability of not getting a sum of <imath>7</imath> is <imath>1-\frac16=\frac56.</imath> Rolling the pair of dice <imath>n</imath> times, the probability of getting a sum of <imath>7</imath> at least once is <imath>1-\left(\frac56\right)^n.</imath>

Therefore, we have <imath>1-\left(\frac56\right)^n>\frac12,</imath> or <cmath>\left(\frac56\right)^n<\frac12.</cmath> Since <imath>\left(\frac56\right)^4<\frac12<\left(\frac56\right)^3,</imath> the least integer <imath>n</imath> satisfying the inequality is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 4}.</imath>

~MRENTHUSIASM

==Solution 2 (Fakesolve)==
Let's try the answer choices. We can quickly find that when we roll <imath>3</imath> dice, either the first and second sum to <imath>7</imath>, the first and third sum to <imath>7</imath>, or the second and third sum to <imath>7</imath>. There are <imath>6</imath> ways for the first and second dice to sum to <imath>7</imath>,  <imath>6</imath> ways for the first and third to sum to <imath>7</imath>, and <imath>6</imath> ways for the second and third dice to sum to <imath>7</imath>. However, we overcounted (but not by much) so we can assume that the answer is <imath>\boxed {\textbf{(C) }4}</imath>.

~Arcticturn

==Solution 3 (Fakesolve)==
We can start by figuring out what the probability is for each die to add up to <imath>7</imath> if there is only <imath>1</imath> roll. We can quickly see that the probability is <imath>\frac16</imath>, as there are <imath>6</imath> ways to make <imath>7</imath> from <imath>2</imath> numbers on a die, and there are a total of <imath>36</imath> ways to add <imath>2</imath> numbers on a die. And since each time we roll the dice, we are adding to the probability, we can conclude that the total probability for rolling a sum of <imath>7</imath> in <imath>n</imath> rolls would be <imath>\frac16</imath><imath>n</imath>. The smallest number that satisfies this is <imath>\boxed {\textbf{(C) }4}</imath>.

~mihikamishra

==Solution 4 (Fakesolve)==
On each roll, there is a <imath>\frac 16</imath> chance of rolling a sum of <imath>7</imath>. You would need <imath>4</imath> of these rolls to get <imath>4 \cdot \frac 16,</imath> which is larger than <imath>\frac 12.</imath> Therefore, the answer is <imath>\boxed {\textbf{(C) }4}.</imath>

~dbnl
